column3: Near-verbatim parallel: God can show the messenger what was promised and remains fully able over its recipients.
Joseph's dream-vision does not clarify a prophet being shown a divinely promised outcome.
The immediate predecessor asks the Lord to show the messenger what the rejecters are promised.
The condemned men's failure to see people they expected does not concern divine disclosure of a promise.
Its warning of a former peoples' day supplies only a broad threatened-outcome setting.
It affirms that God does not fail His promise, grounding confidence in the outcome 23:95 may be shown.
Knowledge that some people deny does not add to the promised showing or divine capacity.
This local rejection of a human messenger supplies background for the threatened outcome, not its disclosure.
Satan's deceptive promises contrast with the reliable divine promise but do not develop being shown it.
It closely repeats the alternative of showing the messenger part of what the rejecters are promised or taking him first.
The repeated fate of earlier peoples gives a general warning context for a promised consequence.
Mocking when seeing a sign is not a parallel to God showing the messenger a promised outcome.
It closely repeats that God may show the messenger part of what is promised, while fulfillment does not depend on his lifespan.
The ancestral saying does not clarify the promise, its visibility, or God's power to realize it.
God's ability to grant victory is a broad instance of effective divine power, without the promise-and-showing frame.
God's ability to remove water offers a local but generic capacity parallel.
Making Jesus an example does not develop the focus's promised outcome or its disclosure.
Reviving dead land visibly demonstrates divine power, but not the promised showing addressed to the messenger.
It closely repeats that the messenger may be shown part of what is promised, with all ultimately returning to God.
Seeking refuge from devils does not clarify the promised showing in the preceding ayah.
The local denial that the promised resurrection is near directly supplies the outcome whose realization God can show.
The elites' social judgments about Noah and his followers do not illuminate divine showing of a promise.
Persistent doubt after clear proofs is a general backdrop for threatened divine consequences.
The believer warns that even part of the messenger's promised consequence may strike his hearers.
The emphatic declaration of divine ability supports the capacity element, though without a promised outcome being shown.
The argument for God's sole divinity does not specifically clarify promised disclosure or its timing.
The rhetorical prospect of punishment or the Hour gives a broad future-crisis parallel without the focus's showing formula.
God's ability to replace and recreate people supports general capacity, not a promise made visible to the messenger.
A dream fulfilled in Joseph's life does not clarify the threatened promise in 23:95.
It explicitly declares God's promise true, directly grounding the certainty of the outcome the messenger may be shown.
The brothers' favorable view of a ruler does not concern divine disclosure or fulfillment of a promise.
This local rejection of Moses and Aaron adds narrative background but not the focus's capacity to show what is promised.
It directly denies that God can fail His promise to His messengers, supporting the certainty behind 23:95.
Attachment to ancestral practice does not clarify the promised outcome or its visibility.
A battle dream in which opponents appear few is a different kind of divinely given sight.
It identifies Hell as the very outcome people were promised, though it does not address showing it to the messenger.
The prisoners' dreams and request for interpretation do not clarify the focus's promised disclosure.
The postmortem barrier and resurrection continue the surah's future-outcome horizon without the showing formula.
Seeing the Day as far away contrasts with the divinely controlled nearness and visibility of a promised event.
The brothers' request for trust concerning Joseph has no material link to a divine promise being shown.
Remembering and interpreting the king's dream does not clarify 23:95's threatened disclosure.
It directly calls God's resurrection promise true while portraying a hearer who dismisses it.
The Israelites' condition for entering the land does not clarify the focus's promise or divine showing.
The immediate instruction to repel evil well gives local context, but not the promised event itself.
The challenge concerning named idols does not develop promised fulfillment or divine capacity to show it.
Both parties in the afterlife attest that their Lord's promises proved true, making fulfillment publicly visible.
The threatened Hell that lies ahead supplies a concrete punishment outcome that can be brought into view.
Noah appeals to the truth of God's promise, while the reply preserves God's authority over its scope and outcome.
Replacing or causing a sign to be forgotten displays general divine ability, not the promised showing in the focus.
The local elites' objection to Noah offers background for a rejected message and its eventual consequence.
Ishmael's truthfulness in promise provides a human analogue of reliable promise-fulfillment, without the showing frame.
Visible variation in provision demonstrates divine governance but does not clarify a promised outcome shown to a messenger.
The statement that Pharaoh's story is a lesson does not materially develop the focus's formula.
The rejecters challenge the timing of a promised event, directly contrasting their demand with God's control of its realization.
God's counted delay explains why a threatened outcome may not be immediately visible without implying inability.
The local elites deny the Hereafter, supplying background for the promise whose reality 23:95 affirms.
It identifies the promised reward as belonging to the Day of Account, though it does not address its disclosure.
Together with the following ayah, it frames the messenger's possible departure before divine retribution is made visible.
The destruction of former communities supplies a general pattern of enacted warning, not the focus's promise-and-showing relation.
The hypocrites' false pledges of support do not clarify God's promise or His ability to show its result.
God's unpreventable ability to replace people directly supports the focus's emphatic capacity, though no promise is named.
The benefits of livestock do not clarify the threatened promise or the messenger's being shown it.
God's power over harm and good is broad authority background, not a specific promised disclosure.
The certainty that God will reduce the earth to barren ground offers an enacted future outcome under emphatic divine control.
When wrongdoers see punishment, their wish to return makes the threatened outcome visibly realized.
Creating additional conveyances does not clarify the focus's promise or capacity to show it.
The prior warning establishes advance notice of consequence but not a promise shown to the messenger.
The inexhaustible provision of Paradise does not clarify the focus's threatened disclosure.
The question about unseen knowledge concerns a person's claim to see the unknown, not God's showing a promise.
The question defining Illiyyun does not develop promise fulfillment, sight, or divine capacity.
God's explicit promise of forgiveness and great reward supports the reliability of divine promises generally.
The election of exemplary servants does not clarify a promised outcome being shown.
It identifies Paradise as what was promised to the returning and watchful, supplying a fulfilled-promise horizon.
God's measured determination is broad support for controlled realization, but does not name a promise or showing.
God's sovereign power to punish or forgive supports His capacity to enact the outcome He promises.
The angels' declaration of standing in ranks does not clarify the focus.
Creation from a drop supplies a visible argument for resurrection, a central promised future outcome.
Claimed guidance through ancestral custom does not illuminate divine disclosure of a promise.
Recognizing error after the fact is a different use of seeing and does not develop 23:95.
The angels' glorification does not concern a promised outcome or its visibility.
The immediate local objection explicitly denies the promised resurrection after death, directly identifying the disputed outcome.
The jinn's mistaken assumption about lies against God does not clarify the focus's promise or capacity.
The warning asks who could protect the people if God's might comes, giving a threatened consequence under divine control.
The request to clarify the cow does not concern a promised result being shown.
Those given knowledge see revelation as truth, a broad reception parallel without the focus's promised-outcome relation.
God's lordship as Creator supports His authority generally but not the specific showing formula.
The declaration that God is knowing and powerful offers only generic support for divine capacity.
Disputing with the Prophet about what he sees is not a parallel to God showing him a promised consequence.
The contrast between Satan's and God's promises supports reliable divine promise only at a general level.
Creation of the heavens and earth is presented as proof that God can raise the dead, directly supporting the promised resurrection outcome.
The staged creation and revival of earth provide visible evidence for the resurrection that rejecters are promised.
Life's shifts from weakness to strength and back show divine power generally, without promise or disclosure.
A person's self-perception of sufficiency does not clarify divine showing or a promised outcome.
The destruction of deniers by the Mighty and Fully Able shows that divine warning is backed by effective power.
The realization that God expands and restricts provision is a broad recognition of divine control, not the focus's promise.
The oath by the promised Day names the fixed future horizon whose arrival God fully controls.
The messenger denies possessing the hastened punishment and assigns judgment to God, directly preserving divine control over its timing.
Creation of the heavens and earth proves God's ability to recreate people and establishes an appointed, unquestionable term.
Mention of Abraham's ancestors does not clarify the focus's promise, sight, or divine power.
God's dominion, giving life and death, and power over all things provide a broad foundation for His ability to realize the promise.
The immediate continuation asks God not to place the messenger among the wrongdoers if he is shown what they are promised, directly completing 23:95's conditional disclosure.
